name: openmsx
why: A thorough MSX emulator with debugger and tooling, a window into 1980s home computing and its odd hardware.

brief.what_it_is: openMSX is an open-source emulator for MSX, the 1980s home computer standard, and related machines. The homepage describes it as 'the MSX emulator that aims for perfection'. It runs MSX software and games from emulated cartridges, disk images, tapes and other media, and it emulates many MSX hardware variants and extensions. Its release history also includes the Spectravideo SVI-318/328, ColecoVision and Sega SG-1000 support. The homepage does not spell out exact inputs and outputs, so the brief keeps this high level.
brief.why_it_exists: The project's stated aim is accuracy: the homepage tagline is 'the MSX emulator that aims for perfection', and the release notes describe work on cycle-accurate VDP timing, floppy (DMK) accuracy and chip-level details. The README is a plain notice that the code is GPL with some files under their own licences, and it is not framed around a problem statement.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage news describes a built-in debugger and a graphical user interface (introduced in 20.0, replacing the OSD menu) for configuring the machine. In 21.0 it added 'setups', which save and load a complete MSX configuration (for example a Philips VG 8020 with an external disk drive, joystick, data recorder and printer) that can be started automatically. Tcl scripting is mentioned in the 0.7.1 and 0.8.1 notes, and reverse/rewind and TAS scripts appear in the 0.8.0 and 0.8.1 notes. The README does not explain the emulation mechanism itself.
brief.install_notes: Downloads are on the homepage: 21.0 for Windows 64-bit (installer or zip), 21.0 for macOS Intel and Apple Silicon, 21.0 for Linux x86 64-bit, 0.15.0 for Android 4.1+ ARM (apk), 19.1 for OpenDingux (opk), and 21.0 source code. The homepage also lists deprecated Catapult and Debugger downloads, and GitHub nightly and Windows community builds. The homepage news says a system with OpenGL 2 support is required. The README points to HTML manuals in doc/manual and release notes in doc/release-notes.txt inside the source tree. I did not see step-by-step build instructions.
brief.standout: It is one of the few MSX emulators approved as a tool-assisted speedrun (TAS) emulator on tasvideos.org (approved 2010), and it has reverse/rewind and TAS scripting built in. Its accuracy claims cover things like VDP access timing and floppy copy protection, not just running software.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage shows openMSX 21.0 released 2025 September 26, following 20.0 (2024 September 22) and 19.1 (2023 August 30). The news also has a 2021 IRC and Discord update. I did not check the GitHub commit history.
brief.caveats: Requires OpenGL 2 or later. The 19.1 release was the last to support systems without OpenGL 2, per the homepage. Windows 32-bit builds are only offered at version 16.0, and the 2007 news says Windows support was once at risk for lack of a maintainer. Catapult and the separate Debugger are marked deprecated on the homepage. The homepage's own documentation and features pages were not reachable through the fetch, so I could not verify a feature list. The GitHub README I got is the source-distribution text, which is thin and has no commands.
quotes: the MSX emulator that aims for perfection
Please note that as of now, a system with OpenGL 2 support is required to run openMSX.

https://github.com/openMSX/openMSX - OK, returned the source-distribution README (thin, points to doc/manual and release notes)

judge.reason: A maintained, accuracy-focused MSX emulator with rewind, scripting, and debugging makes obscure 1980s hardware behavior something you can explore directly.

entry.title: openMSX
entry.tldr: An emulator for the MSX, a 1980s home computer standard, built to be accurate down to chip timing, with a debugger and Tcl scripting.
entry.deeper_look:
openMSX emulates the MSX, a home computer standard from the 1980s, along with many hardware variants and extensions. It runs software from emulated cartridges, disk images and tapes. Its release history also covers related machines: the Spectravideo SVI-318/328, ColecoVision and Sega SG-1000.

The project describes itself as "the MSX emulator that aims for perfection". Release notes mention cycle-accurate VDP (video chip) timing, floppy accuracy and chip-level details. That focus makes it more than a way to run old games: it is a model of how the hardware actually behaved, quirks included.

That accuracy makes it a good place to look inside an old machine. It has a built-in debugger, and a graphical interface (added in 20.0) for configuring the emulated computer. Version 21.0 added "setups", which save a whole machine configuration, such as a Philips VG 8020 with a disk drive, joystick, data recorder and printer, so it can start automatically. Tcl scripting is built in, and the release notes mention reverse/rewind and TAS scripts.

The emulator also has a niche standing: it is one of the few MSX emulators approved for tool-assisted speedrun work on tasvideos.org, approved in 2010.
entry.install:
brew install openmsx
# Needs a system with OpenGL 2 or later. You will also need MSX software or system ROMs to run anything meaningful; the brief does not cover where to get them.

try_this.what_happens: Prints the command-line options so you can see how to choose a machine and load media.

entry.whats_unique: It puts accuracy first, down to VDP access timing and floppy copy protection, and pairs that with a debugger, rewind and Tcl scripting that TAS makers use.
entry.caveats: It needs OpenGL 2 or later, and the brief found no documented commands beyond the manuals bundled in the source tree.
